en: A Letter from Ming-seng Keqin.
On the first day of the ninth month, Keqin, the incumbent of Waguan Jiaosi, respectfully bows and addresses this letter to the Great Monk, the Abbot of Yanliao Tang, and his attendants.
Indeed, the Way flourishes when one finds capable men and declines when it does not.
That human affairs succeed through the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and fail through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is a settled doctrine of antiquity and the present.

Since the teaching of our Buddha entered China, there have been none among the Chinese who have not discussed it; those who take the sūtras as their school and those who take the treatises as their school each have their own masters.
Then, when my master Tiantai appeared during the Chen and Sui dynasties, he [took] the entire Great Canon...
The preface organizes the five periods into eight teachings to elucidate the broad path of this single orthodox tradition,
ensuring that both within and beyond the seas all may be reached by the Buddha’s voice and instruction— how magnificent! During the Dali era of the Tang dynasty,
when the Venerable Xingdao was the tenth patriarch, the Japanese Great Master Saichō attained the Way through him and once personally transcribed this school.
The *Lunshu* (Commentary on the Treatise) states that this marks the beginning of the transmission of our school to Japan.

During the late Tang and Five Dynasties periods, as warfare broke out in the Central Plains, the texts of the various schools were all destroyed by the calamities of war. Many ancestral monasteries were transferred to other sects;
even though several prefectures in Jiangnan remained unchanged due to the protection of Qian Liu, such as the Waguan Monastery in Jinling, these were no longer possessed by our school.
The family tradition was nearly on the verge of extinction. Then, when the son of Qiu, King Zhongyi, dispatched an envoy eastward to seek the *Kanjur*, the Korean Master Gao brought it to court.
Upon the Song dynasty’s accession to the throne, with its sage ruler and worthy ministers, Heaven also produced the Venerable Fazhi in person;
he supplemented the fragmented scrolls, searched out what had been lost, and compiled and clarified these magnificent teachings.

However, it was during his time that the tradition was revived. In Japan, there was a Dharma-bridge Master (Hōkyō Jōshi) named Enchin, who heard of his [Zhiyi’s] Way and presented twenty-seven points of doubt for resolution.
He went to Jizhao to inquire about them, and the Venerable One answered each question as it arose, like the brilliant splendor of stars and the sun.
I wonder if his calligraphy still survives today; he crossed to the south during the reign of Emperor Ningzong. Jun.
Dharma Master Lingmo previously transmitted the Yoga Tantras from Japan to China, where he visited Master Yu Kang at Beifeng and Mount Ling;

he too thoroughly mastered their essential tenets, and both were great figures of their respective eras. Observing the teachings of the former Buddhas, one sees that they were initially transmitted from Tiantai to Japan;
examining the records, we find that sovereigns of the Tang and Song dynasties engaged in frequent exchanges with Japan.
Cultivating friendly relations like those between father and son, it is no wonder that our disciples have come to seek the Way with such singular devotion.
When the rulers of China behold their loyalty and good faith, and rejoice in the ritual propriety and righteousness of their nation, they consequently value these friendly ties all the more.
Otherwise, why is it that among the many nations of the Eastern Sea, none are as close and cordial as Japan? This, then, is the work of Heaven.

The disciples of Tiantai not only widely propagated the Buddha’s teachings to benefit sentient beings, but also assisted the King’s transformation of the people so that his benevolence might cover all subjects.

Previously, when the Mongols illegitimately entered the Central Kingdom, extinguished the Song, and established themselves as sovereigns, Japan was incensed by the barbarian hordes’ conduct, which was like that of dogs and pigs, and thus became their enemy. From that time on, the followers of our school ceased to appear there.
It is China alone that, since the advent of Chan Buddhism, has seen ships crossing the seas in constant succession, one after another;
yet people there were diligent and skeptical, wondering why those from the same country differed so much between past and present, or why their fortunes varied between success and failure.
Now, our Great Ming Emperor, with his divine sagacity and martial prowess, has driven the various barbarians beyond the borders and restored the ancestral lands of the former Song dynasty.
Since the Central Plains had been pacified and the borders were likewise tranquil, he then directed his spirit toward the Inner Scriptures (Buddhism), desiring to revitalize them.

Therefore, on the first day of the first month of this spring’s moon-festival period, he issued an edict for more than one thousand eminent masters of the Three Sects from throughout the realm to establish a Great Universal Salvation Assembly at Jiangshan Temple in the capital.
The Emperor himself observed the fast and maintained ritual purity for one month, while prohibiting slaughter throughout the empire.

Furthermore, he personally led the civil and military officials to the altar to perform prostrations; he also commissioned the composition of musical lyrics and ordered the master musicians to perform them as offerings to the Buddha.
When the multitude witnessed auspicious light illuminating the heavens and rain falling at night in five colors, shaped like pearls and jade beads, the Emperor was greatly delighted.
The Chan Master Bai’an of the Heavenly Realm, a venerable elder of our school, was summoned several times to engage in dialogues concerning the sutras and treatises.
The Emperor’s decree being issued, Waguan Temple was restored as a Tiantai teaching monastery, and the assembly recommended Dharma Master Qin to preside over it.
Previously, over the course of two years, the Emperor had three times dispatched envoys; the Prince of Kansai from Japan had also personally offered it [the temple] at those times.
At that moment, because Zule had entered the court to offer congratulations, the Emperor summoned Chan Master Tianning to serve as its abbot, whereupon Zule expounded the teachings at Waguan.
The Abbot of Jiaosi Temple, Keqin, was commanded: "My previous three dispatches of envoys to Japan were intended to seek an audience with Emperor Chōmei.
That the one from Kansai came here was not my original intention;

because the border prohibitions do not allow monks to pass through, I wish to entrust you two to go secretly and inform him of my intent, saying: 'The Middle Kingdom has changed its sovereign and established [a new dynasty]...'"
The dynasty is named the Great Ming, and the first year of its reign is designated Hongwu. Because they have come here by imperial decree, those from the countryside have all been blocked at Guansi.
We two, being in close proximity, inform Your Majesty of this. The people of your great kingdom have repeatedly raided our borders;

Your Majesty ought to prohibit this. Trade has been obstructed; Your Majesty ought to facilitate it. Let us follow the precedents of the Tang and Song dynasties and restore friendly relations as before. Furthermore, he commanded—
The Emperor said: "I have heard that from the sovereign down to his ministers and all those above and below, they all know to revere the Buddha and honor the monks.
It is none other than you monks who are sufficient to inspire confidence in them. There are monks of both the Chan and Teaching schools who wish to seek the Way in the Middle Kingdom;
I permit them all to come without restriction. Only you two shall go; do not neglect this task. He then bestowed upon them the three robes and eighteen essential items of pure requisites.
Furthermore, fearing that we might arrive there and find our speech unintelligible, he selected Chan monks from the eastern regions who were residing in China:
the Elder Chunting Shou of Dongshan and the Abbot Quanzhong Xun of Zhongzhu. Because these two had experience in traveling to various quarters, he appointed them as his assistants for the journey.
He cautioned them, saying: "To be diligent in one's mission is what the Buddha taught; let us ensure that we do not fail to contribute to the cause."
To violate the Buddha’s precepts for the sake of the Buddha’s teaching, even at the cost of death, I would not do so; this is my observance of the precept against falsehood.

Since His Majesty has now deemed me trustworthy and dispatched me, it is my observance of the precept against lying. To exhort others to prohibit raiding is my observance of the precept against stealing.
By cultivating friendly relations between the two nations so that merchants may travel freely and the people may live in peace, military conflict shall cease.
Furthermore, the precept against killing is a boundary of the Dharma; to uphold the Buddha’s precepts while serving as an imperial envoy is to act as a messenger of the Buddha.
Therefore, on the day I received this commission, I applied myself diligently and did not decline it.

How much more so now that I have heard that Mount Tiantai is the foremost monastery in the land—how could one who stands at its head, belonging to a prominent clan of the nation, not exert themselves to support those of the same lineage?

If you are willing to assist me in accomplishing this task, then the practitioners of the Tiantai school will be able to save the affairs of both countries, and the rulers of those two nations will surely have expectations for our school.
Although Qin had already prepared for this and did not decline, the commentaries and records of the successive patriarchs had been destroyed during the Five Dynasties period;
furthermore, even though Master Guan had come from Goryeo, he was still lacking in many essential materials. Therefore, I set out.
He consulted with the leading temple administrators and was permitted to bring [the scriptures] back to his country.
Later, upon reading those books, one would inevitably say, "This particular book was obtained by such-and-such a person and came from such-and-such a source.

Thus, the merit of restoring the Buddhist canon was not solely that of Master Gao-li (Goryeo) and Guanshi (Guanshi). Furthermore, because of this, those who study the teachings have long ceased to feel weary.
Although it was not yet clear that he would pass away later, because I departed and he arrived, the lineage of masters such as Tancheng and Huirong would have a successor.
Because of this, I did not decline his request; thus, on the twentieth day of the fifth month, I set sail for Siming, arriving at Wu Island on the third day and reaching Hakata on the fifth.
Above, there were no violent winds; below, there were no treacherous waves. If only... [the rest of the passage follows].
If the mind were not as it is, how could the Buddhas, Patriarchs, and divine spirits have allowed such security and such swiftness?
On the day we reached the shore, I heard that the state was about to dispatch an army to recover the lands of Guansi and unify them under one house;
I thought to myself that my task would be accomplished without further exertion. Unbeknownst to me, they caused me to remain and stay at Shengfu Temple, where I traded my robes for food.
I have been eating while standing on tiptoe awaiting my fate for over a hundred days, yet still I remain in deep uncertainty, having received no report.
I do not know what the Great State intends to discuss with me in its summons, nor why it hesitates regarding me and keeps me waiting.

Furthermore, when even a single envoy from a close relative state enters the Middle Kingdom, the government immediately provides him with sauce and food, and prepares carriages and horses for land travel, as well as boats and oars for water travel; how much more so should this be the case for one such as I?

Upon arriving at the capital, he was lodged at Huìtóng Monastery; every third day there was a banquet, and the envoys from the north and south who had come to offer congratulations were all seated below him.
When the Emperor personally attended the court audience to receive him, he treated him with such affection that not even a hair’s breadth of suspicion arose. Why was this?

The Emperor considered that although the monk had come from the land of his ancestors, Japan maintained an ancient friendship with the former Song dynasty, and thus he was treated as one of his own kin.
It is because of the heart. Regarding the division of the realm among the various kings of the West, the treatment accorded to the ancestors has traditionally been extended to the envoys from Japan;
though we have long been diligent in this regard, we certainly did not expect a formal recompense as was granted to the ancestors.

Yet, if even a single envoy sent by Your Majesty desires to communicate your commands to the four quarters, and since our Great Country possesses the virtue of ritual integrity and righteousness, we shall [respond accordingly].
They admired Song and hated Hu; yet, because they could serve the Buddha and revere the monks, they came with singular trust in us.
Now, instead of trusting them, they treat them with suspicion—thus the monastics are not as diligent as the laity, and these several individuals are not as worthy as one Patriarch.
They came to China with propriety and yet met with the arrogance of Japan. Shall I merely return their lives? I have often pondered this.
I have heard that the Venerable Master possesses complete Way and perfected virtue; his merit is profound and his wisdom sufficient.

Furthermore, he is a man of great lineage in the realm, and many high officials and ministers place their trust and submission in him. I humbly hope that you will, on the one hand, consider the safety and peril of the state, and on the other, reflect upon the flourishing or decline of the religious tradition, and that you will convey these matters with a sense of diligent urgency.
The King’s high minister then again brought him forward to have an audience with [the Emperor], so that he would not fail what he had previously reported.
Not only did Qin gain a reputation for being trustworthy, but the Upādhyāya also acquired a reputation for excellence.
Thus Qin said: "The Way flourishes when one obtains capable people and declines when one loses them; human affairs succeed through action and fail through inaction."

This is what is meant by being "covered. Having been detained for so long, my resources for sustenance are nearly exhausted; I have therefore requested the Elder of Dongshan to go and expedite this matter.
Although we have not met in person as our karmic conditions place us in different locations, my heart’s devotion to you has never ceased to be intimate.
Thus, I venture to present these words to your presence, hoping you will not cast me aside as a stranger, but will treat me as one of your old disciples from Tiantai.
This scroll of a sacred image is the brushwork of a renowned master of the former Song dynasty, with a eulogy by the Chan Master Xutang;
I respectfully submit it along with the calligraphy. The details regarding the incomplete portions of the memorial inscription are listed separately for your perusal.
I await your command from within the palace, as my longing from the seaside is most earnest and cannot be suppressed.
Keqin bows his head to the ground at Tianting Monastery; Zuanchan joins him in bowing.
Hereafter, the number of lost Tiantai doctrinal texts is set forth as follows.

*The Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā of Mount Nanyue*, two fascicles (brought to China by the Japanese monk Jō in the third year of the Xianping era of the Song dynasty; subsequently lost and no longer extant);
*The Gate of the Forty-two Syllables*, two fascicles; *The Gate of Non-contentious Practice*, two fascicles.
*The Gate of Contemplation of the Threefold Wisdom*, one fascicle (the same applies hereafter). *Commentary on the Essentials of Successive Meditation*,
by Zhiyi of Tiantai.
*Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, twenty fascicles; *Commentary on the Maitreya-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*, five fascicles;
*Explanation of the Meaning of All Sūtras through the Contemplation of the Mind*, one fascicle;
*Commentary on the Maitreya-upapatti-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, two fascicles.
*Chánmén zhāng* (One fascicle; the same applies to all subsequent entries):
*Bānruò xíngfǎ*, *Zá guānxíng rùdào dàzhǐ*, *Wǔ fāngbiàn mén*, *Qī fāngbiàn yì*.
The Meaning of the Seven Learners; The Meanings of the One, Two, Three, and Four Bodies;
The Ritual for the Dharma-Gate; An Essential Summary of the Chan Gate;
A Commentary on the Meaning of the Amitābha Sūtra; A Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
One fascicle of *The General Meaning of the Eight Teachings* by Zhang’an; the *Record of Nanyue*;
and the *Biography of Dharma Master Zhi guan*.

*Jingxi Zhiguan Souyao Ji* (Jingxi’s Record of the Essential Points of Stopping and Contemplation), ten fascicles; *Niepan Houfen Shu* (Commentary on the Latter Part of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra), one fascicle (the same applies hereafter);
*Shou Pusa Jie Wen* (Text for Bestowing the Bodhisattva Precepts); *Zhiguan Wenzhu* (Text and Phrases of Stopping and Contemplation).
The Ritual for the Vaipulya Sūtras to Supplement Deficiencies is fully set forth above.
Written on the [blank] day of the ninth month in the fifth year of Hongwu by Keqin of Waguan.
The Tiantai lineage of patriarchs:
the High Ancestor, Venerable Nāgārjuna; the Second Ancestor, the Venerable of the Northern Qi;
the Third Ancestor, the Venerable of Mount Heng; and the Fourth Ancestor, the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai.
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Zhang’an; the Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Fǎhuá;
the Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Tiāngōng; the Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Zuǒxī;
and the Ninth Patriarch, Venerable Jīngxī (the above constitute the Nine Patriarchs).
The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Xingdao (who was the Japanese Great Master Saichō, also known as Hōshi);
the Eleventh Patriarch, Venerable Zhixing; the Twelfth Patriarch, Venerable Zhengding;
the Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Miaoshuo; and the Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gaolun.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Jingguang; the Sixteenth Patriarch, Venerable Baoyun;
the Seventeenth Patriarch, Venerable Fazhi (the above constitute the seventeen patriarchs);
Master Nanping and Master Cibian.
Master Chexi, Master Zhuanan, Master Beifeng, Master Shanyuan,
Master Yunmeng, and Master Zantang.
From Master Wuan and Master Yuanpu (the latter being the dharma-heir of Keqin) down to Master Yuanpu, there are twenty-seven transmissions in total.
Prior to Zhuanan, all collateral lines lacked transmission; however, among the ten people in the lineage of Beifeng, three or two [remained].

Although these lineages were transmitted equally to China, the Śānyuán (Shan Yuan) tradition became particularly prominent; nevertheless, their fundamental tenets and ritual protocols originated from a single source.
The monk Kèqín, successor to the patriarch, respectfully submits this memorial:
on the fifth year of the Hongwǔ era, the *rénzǐ* year, corresponding to the first year of the *Chángqìng* reign of Emperor Wénzhōng of the Southern Court.
Northern Dynasty: In the fifth year of the En’an era during the reign of Emperor Ōgimachi (Jōkei), Prince Son’ō of Shōren’in served as the *Zasu* (Head Abbot) of the Tendai school.
The *Xù Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo* states: "In the tenth month of winter in the fourth year of the Hongwu era of the Ming dynasty, the King of Japan..."
Lianghuai dispatched his monk Zu to the court to present a memorial, a letter of introduction, a horse, and local products as tribute, accompanied by nine other monks.
An imperial edict granted them fine silks in response.
The *Fǎmén Shū* (Book of Fǎmén), fascicle 146, states: "In the second year after the Emperor Gāozōng ascended the throne, he sent the envoy Yang Zai..."
An imperial edict was issued to King Ryanghwa, granting him a sealed letter (*xi-shu*). Ryanghwa dispatched his minister, the monk Sengzu, to present a memorial acknowledging himself as a subject.
He sent the monks Zhongyou and Keqin, along with seven others, to escort [the envoy] back to his country;
this was in the fourth year of Hongwu.

The *Tushu Bian* (Compendium of Books), fascicle 50, states: In the second year of the Hongwu era, Japanese pirates raided the coastal prefectures and counties of Shandong and further attacked Huai'an.
In the third year, an imperial edict was bestowed to admonish their king, Ryōnō.
In the fifth year, the monk Zuchan from Tiantong Temple in Mingzhou and the monk Wuyi from Waguan Temple in Nanjing were dispatched to offer exhortations. The king sent envoys to accompany them.
Two monks entered the imperial court as tribute.
The *Collected Works* composed by the Emperor Gao (the *Collected Works of Ming Taizu Zhu Yuanzhang*) states:

"When our dynasty first reclaimed the Central Lands, we were determined to establish deep relations with Japan; this was the purpose of the mission undertaken by the two monks Kōkin and Chūyū" (and so forth).
The *Jiuling Shanfang Ji* states: The monk Chan (the patriarch Chan of Tianning Monastery) was sent as an envoy to Japan and obtained a stone inkstone from Qinglong.
He requested a colophon for it, which reads: "Praiseworthy is this inkstone produced in the Eastern Barbarians; it possesses a spiritual source and knows its proper destination.
Alas for those people of the world—why do they not reflect on this?"
From the *Mengguan ji* (Anthology of Dream Contemplations), titled "Sending Qín Wúyì as Envoy to Japan" (compiled by Shì Rúlán of Fùchūn):
The Great Ming establishes its state like those of Yú and Táng; Myriads of nations bring jade and silk to the Hall of Light.
From among five hundred monks, an envoy-monk was selected; Heeding the imperial decree, he traveled directly to the eastern land of Fusang.
To the east of Fusang, misty waters stretch afar; a million towers and pavilions rise from within the sea.
To the west lie coral trees and *zhū* trees, where the Red Pines grow amidst jade ridges, golden peaks, and azure clouds.
Its layered walls and sturdy ramparts are stronger than iron; its robes, caps, rites, and music are transmitted from the central capital.
Lou Ban vainly speaks of the envoy from the Co family; Yet the ashes remain unmoved, and the books of the Dark Zhou are white.
The high jade cords descend upon the Ba River Pass; A divine plum from the heavens is transplanted to the northern wilds.
The Eight-Roll Divine Master understands how to tame dragons; A child of ten years knows how to train horses.
Since the Sun-clan first opened the borders, Treading the earth, none dared to call themselves Heavenly Kings.
One Sovereign and four Ministers offered counsel, both in harmony and in dispute; For a hundred generations, the main and branch lines have flourished together.
In studying, they do not prize discourses on kingship or hegemony; From high to low, they know only to honor the transformation of the Buddha.
I still recall the remnants of the five Li clans after the devastation of war; Fully upholding Your Majesty’s decree, we shall restore the Central Kingdom.
Our old friend is indeed an image of our own lineage; The Northern Peak transmits the seal of the lamp through six generations.
This journey is not merely to boast of skill in diplomatic representation; It is essential to spread the profound wind [of the Dharma] and assist the King’s enterprise.
With my wandering staff and bowl, I bid farewell to the Nine Palaces; In the fourth month, the great sail unfurls as the south wind blows.
A pair of soaring dragons welcome me with white spray; The celestial cock crows once, and the eastern sky turns crimson.
I sing that the white clouds stretch ten thousand miles across the heavens; Such indeed should be the way for a man to live his life.
Gazing at the Autumnal Waves from the Waguan Pavilion, I await your return to report [the news] to the Son of Heaven.
*Fozu Tongji* states:
Nanying Fanzhen (a dharma heir of Siming), Cibian Congjian, and Dongxi Zexiang.
Zhuan-an Ke-guan; Bei-feng Zong-yin (the Japanese missionary Junrei alone);
Liyuan Jue-xian. *Fozu Tongji* states:
Yunmeng is truly a vast marsh; Zhandang’s nature is clear and still; Wuan is fundamentally non-existent.
